response: The wind had howled for three days, rattling the thick glass of the lantern room and throwing salt spray high enough to coat the walkways in a slick, white crust. Now, the sea was an exhausted gray, heaving in slow, sullen swells. Elias tightened his wool coat against the biting chill as he descended the spiraling iron stairs, the rhythmic *clack-clack* of his boots echoing in the damp stone tower. He stepped out onto the lower gallery to assess the damage. Kelp was strewn across the rocks like discarded ribbons, and a wooden crate, splintered and waterlogged, was wedged against the base of the sea wall. As he moved to clear it, a flash of dull green caught his eye. Half-buried in a tangle of seaweed was a glass bottle, thick and old. Elias knelt, his joints protesting the damp cold, and picked it up. Inside, protected from the fury of the storm, rested a tightly rolled piece of paper, tied with a faded crimson thread. He held it up to the pale morning light, tracing the outline of the paper with a calloused thumb, the vast, empty ocean suddenly feeling very small and very close.
